source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles (Artificial Intelligence 32(1):57-95), as restated in Wassermann (2000)
finding: Founding theory. A conflict set is a set of 'component ok' assumptions that cannot all hold given the system description and observation. A diagnosis is a minimal set of components that, if assumed faulty, restores consistency. Reiter's theorem: diagnoses are exactly the minimal hitting sets of the collection of minimal conflict sets.
numbers: Worked example: circuit with components X,Y,Z, observation not-C and not-F gives one minimal conflict {okY, okZ}; hitting sets {Y},{Z},{Y,Z}; only {Y} and {Z} are diagnoses. Proposition: a diagnosis exists iff SD plus OBS is consistent.
quote: A diagnosis is a minimal set such that ASS minus the set is consistent with the observation.
limits: Read via Wassermann's restatement, not the 1987 paper itself. Propositional simplification of Reiter's first-order setting.
agent_relevance: Gives our agent a precise rule: suspects are the smallest sets that touch every contradiction found so far. Fits S5 (locate fault) and the search over suspects.

source: Reiter (1987) HS-tree algorithm, as described in Pill, Quaritsch & Wotawa (2016)
finding: Reiter's HS-tree is a breadth-first tree. Each non-leaf node is labelled with a conflict not yet hit by the edge labels on the path from the root (h(n)). One child per component in that conflict. A node with no unhit conflict is a hitting-set candidate; a candidate that is a superset of an earlier leaf is closed. Subset checks prune non-minimal conflicts. Cardinality limits are cheap: only nodes with small h(n) are built, and the limit can be raised later by continuing the tree.
numbers: Running example SCS={{1,2},{1,2,5},{2,3,4},{2,4,5}} gives minimal hitting sets {2}, {1,4}, {1,3,5}.
limits: Pill et al. use the Greiner-corrected version (HS-DAG) in their tests, not the 1987 original.
agent_relevance: Breadth-first order means smallest-cardinality suspect sets come out first, matching a fewest-faults-first rule for an agent.

source: Greiner, Smith & Wilkerson (1989) A correction to the algorithm in Reiter's theory of diagnosis (Artificial Intelligence 41(1):79-88), as reported by Gainer-Dewar & Vera-Licona 2016
finding: Reiter's original tree algorithm is incomplete. What it returns is minimal, but in some situations it misses minimal hitting sets. The repair reuses nodes that have the same path label set h(n), so the structure becomes a directed acyclic graph (HS-DAG) instead of a tree.
numbers: No complexity analysis known: the survey authors are not aware of a formal complexity analysis. Depth can be bounded to search only hitting sets up to a given size.
quote: Greiner et al. showed in [60] that this algorithm is incomplete; the hitting sets it generates are guaranteed to be minimal
limits: Seen only through survey text; the 1989 paper itself was not opened. The trigger is non-minimal conflicts used as node labels.
agent_relevance: Lesson for the agent: if the conflicts fed to the search are not minimal, naive search can silently lose a valid suspect set. Shrink every conflict to a minimal one first.

source: Greiner et al. (1989) fix as explained in Pill, Quaritsch & Wotawa (2016)
finding: HS-DAG fixes 'minor but serious flaws' in Reiter's original. Main idea: when the children of a node are created, look for an existing node with the same h(n) and reuse it as the target of the new edge, rather than making a duplicate subtree.
numbers: Walk-through on the running example: root n0 labelled {1,2}; node for {2} hits everything and is reported; node for {2,3} is a superset of a found hitting set and is closed; final DAG reports {2},{1,4},{1,3,5}.
limits: Reuse needs a lookup over node label sets, which is the extra cost HST later removes.
agent_relevance: Reuse of repeated partial hypotheses is caching: do not re-explore a suspect set already reached by another route.

source: Wotawa (2001) A variant of Reiter's hitting-set algorithm (Information Processing Letters 79(1)), as reported in two sources
finding: HST: Wotawa changes the construction so nodes that Reiter's method would later prune are never built. It numbers components and only expands children with labels in a fixed range, like subset enumeration. This cuts set-containment checks and makes the DAG generalisation unnecessary, so it is a tree again.
numbers: In the 2016 benchmark HST was usually faster than HS-DAG in the mid-size group, but it was the only algorithm that scaled worse and used much more memory above about 20 components in the disjoint-conflict test (TSA1).
limits: Wotawa 2001 itself was not opened (publisher page returned 403).
agent_relevance: A fixed ordering of suspects can replace duplicate checking, so the agent never revisits the same set.

source: Gainer-Dewar & Vera-Licona (2016) The minimal hitting set generation problem: algorithms and computation (benchmark of about 20 algorithms)
finding: Survey and benchmark of about two dozen minimal hitting set algorithms. MMCS and RS (Murakami and Uno) and HTC-BDD (Toda) were far faster than the rest, including Reiter/Greiner HS-DAG and Wotawa HST.
numbers: Each run capped at 3600 s. HTC-BDD 4 to 10 times faster than its closest rivals on many inputs but often used up the 32 GB of memory and has no cutoff mode. HER2+.SHORT: 122 elements, 534 sets, 128,833,310 minimal hitting sets, yet only 26,436 of size 7 or less. MHS2 parallel algorithm showed a 2.33x speedup.
limits: Inputs are biology networks and data-mining sets, not diagnosis conflicts. Xeon E5-2630v3 workstation. No algorithm completed full enumeration on any HER2+ family.
agent_relevance: The number of minimal hitting sets can explode. An agent must cap suspect-set size (cutoff) rather than enumerate all.

source: Gainer-Dewar & Vera-Licona (2016) The minimal hitting set generation problem: algorithms and computation (complexity)
finding: Deciding whether a hitting set of a given size exists is NP-complete. Generating all minimal hitting sets is the monotone dualisation problem, with no known output-polynomial algorithm. Bounded cardinality makes it manageable.
numbers: Berge's algorithm is not output-polynomial (Takata bounds). HS-DAG and HST can restrict to bounded cardinality by limiting depth.
limits: Worst-case claims; real diagnosis inputs are often easier.
agent_relevance: Justifies a hard budget on the width and depth of the agent's suspect search.

source: Pill, Quaritsch & Wotawa (2016) On the practical performance of minimal hitting set algorithms from a diagnostic perspective (IJPHM 7(2))
finding: Empirical comparison of HS-DAG, HST, GDE, two Boolean algorithms, Staccato and two direct SAT encodings on artificial and ISCAS'85 conflict sets. No single winner. GDE best below about 30 components or 10 ms; Boolean algorithms lead from about 30 components and beat GDE by more than an order of magnitude beyond 200 components; HS-DAG catches up around 500 ms and is close to GDE for large conflict collections; SAT variants about two orders of magnitude slower than the intermediate group.
numbers: Limits 300 s and 2 GiB, MacBook Pro 2011. TSA1: disjoint conflicts, |SCS|=3, |COMP| 3 to 1000, 20 samples per point. TSA2: random conflicts, |COMP|=100, max cardinality 3. TSR1-TSR4: ISCAS circuits with 202 to 880 gates, 100 samples each, up to triple faults. Boolean without its split-heuristic optimisation: advantage border fell from about 500 conflicts to about 20.
limits: Python implementations; conflicts supplied as pre-computed cardinality-sorted sets, so conflict computation cost is excluded. Staccato could not finish the smallest TSA2 samples.
agent_relevance: Boolean bookkeeping beats tree search only when all conflicts are known in advance. Our agent finds conflicts one at a time, which favours the tree style.

source: Pill, Quaritsch & Wotawa (2011) From conflicts to diagnoses (DX'11), as cited by Shchekotykhin et al. 2015
finding: Earlier comparison. The binary BHS-tree of Lin and Jiang (2003) was reported not generally favourable over HS-tree algorithms, especially when only a limited set of diagnoses is wanted.
numbers: No figures in the sources opened.
limits: Second-hand; the 2011 paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: Favour plain breadth-first search when only the few best suspect sets are needed.

source: Rodler (2019) Towards optimizing Reiter's HS-Tree for sequential diagnosis
finding: HS-Tree is sound, complete and best-first, but is used statelessly: after each new measurement the tree is thrown away and rebuilt. DynamicHS keeps the tree and updates it: conflicts can only shrink, diagnoses can only grow, so existing nodes are pruned, relabelled or extended, never reduced.
numbers: Toy example: HS-Tree needs 14/0/9 calls (conflict search / redundancy check / consistency check), DynamicHS 6/4/5. First real-KB test: DynamicHS saved 59% of expensive reasoner calls and 42% of running time on average, and was faster in all observed sessions.
quote: HS-Tree per se does not encompass any specific provisions for being used in an iterative way.
limits: Workshop paper, preliminary. Reiter asked in 1987 whether the old tree could be reused after a measurement; the paper says no earlier algorithm answered that.
agent_relevance: After each test result, update the suspect tree instead of restarting search: the S7 loop of test, update, re-rank.

source: Rodler (2020) DynamicHS: Streamlining Reiter's hitting-set tree for sequential diagnosis (arXiv 2012.11078)
finding: Full evaluation of DynamicHS against HS-Tree on real faulty ontologies. Same solutions, less time. DynamicHS was faster in 99.4% of diagnosis scenarios and 96% of single sessions.
numbers: Median savings per scenario 52%, maximum 75%. Median by heuristic: 50% ENT, 52% SPL, 52% MPS (not significantly different). Hardest cases per scenario: median saving 64%, maximum 89%; HS-Tree took up to 9 times as long in a single session. 20 sessions per scenario; Wilcoxon signed rank tests significant in about 97% of scenarios. ld in {2,4,6,10,20,30}; median savings 45-51% across ld. Two scenarios lost slightly (median -2% and -3%), never by more than 0.8 s and 12 s.
limits: Knowledge-base debugging only (OWL ontologies, EXPTIME to 2-NEXPTIME consistency checks); random fault probabilities. Trades memory for time; uses only minimal conflicts as labels.
agent_relevance: Evidence that keeping search state across test rounds pays when each check is costly, as an LLM call is.

source: Rodler (2020) DynamicHS: soundness conditions for HS-Tree (same paper)
finding: Fault probabilities must put each component below 0.5 for best-first HS-Tree to stay sound (only minimal diagnoses returned). Fix: scale all probabilities by a constant c in (0, 0.5). A footnote says that using only minimal conflicts as node labels avoids the Greiner et al. 1989 problem.
numbers: Reasoner calls ranked easy/medium/hard: hard calls at least 4 and up to over 100 times costlier than medium and easy ones.
quote: each system component must be more likely to be nominal than to be faulty
limits: Assumes independent component faults.
agent_relevance: If the agent weights suspects by prior, keep each prior under 0.5 or best-first search may return non-minimal sets.

source: Shchekotykhin, Jannach & Schmitz (2015) MergeXplain: fast computation of multiple conflicts for diagnosis (IJCAI)
finding: HS-tree usually asks a conflict finder (QuickXplain, QXP) for one conflict per node, restarting each time. MergeXplain splits the constraint set in halves and returns several minimal conflicts per run.
numbers: On CSP and spreadsheet benchmarks up to 54% faster when searching 5 diagnoses (costasArray-13: 1,379,842 ms to 629,366 ms), but 11% slower on queens-8 and 5% slower on one spreadsheet. On generated problems: about 20-30% gains when conflicts sit at random positions, up to 75% when unlucky for QXP, and small losses when conflicts are clustered. Parallel version adds modest further gains.
limits: Consistency-check time simulated in the generated tests (quadratic in size, capped at 10 ms). Single-conflict cases can get slightly slower.
agent_relevance: Getting several conflicts from one probe call is the key cost saver; an LLM prompt that returns several minimal contradictions per call mirrors this.

source: Felfernig, Schubert & Zehentner (2012) An efficient diagnosis algorithm for inconsistent constraint sets (FastDiag, AIEDAM 26(1))
finding: Computing a diagnosis of cardinality n through hitting sets needs at least n minimal conflicts. FastDiag finds one preferred minimal diagnosis directly, by divide and conquer, with the effort of finding one conflict. In tests it beat QuickXplain-based HS-DAG, both breadth-first and best-first.
numbers: CLib configuration KB, 34 variables, about 65 constraints; requirement sets of 5, 7, 10, 15; first diagnosis, first 5, first 10 and all. Mann-Whitney: best-first vs breadth-first HSDAG p=6.6e-5; FastDiag vs breadth-first p<2.4e-7; FastDiag vs best-first p=0.12 (no difference in ranking precision).
limits: One benchmark KB on a 2.66 GHz Core2 Quad; breadth-first HS-DAG had the worst precision at predicting the user's chosen diagnosis.
agent_relevance: If only one good fault set is needed, go direct (remove half the suspects, test, recurse) instead of building the full tree.

source: Shchekotykhin, Fleiss, Rodler & Friedrich (2012) Direct computation of diagnoses for ontology debugging
finding: When ontologies hold many conflicts, pre-computing them is infeasible. Inv-HS-Tree calls the direct Inv-QuickXplain n times to find diagnoses without conflicts, and succeeds where HS-Tree fails.
numbers: OAEI 2011 Conference suite: 286 alignments; 140 consistent and coherent, 122 incoherent, 26 inconsistent, 8 where HermiT did not finish in 2 hours. 146 analysed; both methods got the requested 1, 9 and 30 diagnoses for 133. In 13 cases only Inv-HS-Tree finished, e.g. csa-conference-ekaw: HS-Tree found only 1 diagnosis in 2 h; Inv-HS-Tree took 11,257 / 31,010 / 62,823 ms for 1 / 9 / 30 diagnoses.
limits: Ontology matching only; HS-Tree can be faster when conflicts are few.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: tree search stalls when conflicts are numerous or large; keep a direct fallback.

source: Wassermann (2000) Local diagnosis
finding: Shows that consistency-based diagnosis is a kernel semi-revision from belief change: conflicts are kernels, the incision function picks one element from each kernel, diagnoses are the minimal incisions. Restricting to the part of the system relevant to the observation lets diagnosis run on a smaller set.
numbers: Theory paper; no experiments.
limits: Propositional, small examples.
agent_relevance: Link to belief revision: give up the least belief per contradiction. Also supports focusing the search on the relevant slice of the problem.

source: Plank & Wotawa (2026) Using SLMs and LLMs for diagnosis (DX 2026)
finding: 13 language models were given a plain-text description of circuits and heating systems and asked for the faulty components. No hitting-set search; the prompt did not ask for subset-minimal diagnoses. Bigger models were better, but all still hallucinated.
numbers: Weighted score (max 2.0): Gemini 2.5 Flash 1.846, Mistral Large 1.832, Llama 4 Scout 17B 1.526, best small model Mistral 7B v0.3 1.235, TinyLlama 1.1B 0.314. Hit rate (correctness score 2): 79.5%, 76.9%, 38.5%, 25.6%. Hallucination rate: 20.5%, 15.4%, 7.7%, 61.5%; most small models above 70%, Llama 3.2 1B 94.9%. 7 systems, manual scoring.
limits: Small systems, manual scoring, only freely available models. Phi-2's good Powertrain score was judged textbook overlap, not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: Baseline: unaided LLMs get the fault right about 80% of the time on small systems at best. A hitting-set scaffold must beat this on larger ones.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) Are diagnostic concepts within the reach of LLMs? (DX 2025)
finding: Closest LLM use of the Reiter pipeline. Prompts for three steps on Boolean circuits: generate MSO sets, evaluate them against observations to get conflicts, then generate minimal diagnoses (the hitting-set step) from the conflicts. Models: gpt-4o-mini, o1, o3-mini.
numbers: o3-mini: F1 = 0.917 +/- 0.249 on conflict generation and 0.784 +/- 0.322 on minimal diagnoses generation. Diagnosis generation degraded as examples grew; examples had up to 6 MSOs, 6 conflicts and 165 diagnoses (Example 9). o1 best at conflicts. Ground truth from the Fault Diagnosis Toolbox and an exact minimal hitting set implementation. Examples hand-made and unseen in training.
quote: at this point, LLMs do not provide an alternative to diagnosis algorithms
limits: Small hand-built examples. The authors say LLMs do not provide an alternative to diagnosis algorithms; quality varies between runs; cost and time unbounded.
agent_relevance: LLMs find conflicts well but weaken at the hitting-set step. So compute hitting sets by code and use the LLM to find conflicts.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) incidence matrix and conflict-count findings
finding: Incidence matrix step: o1 and o3-mini near perfect; gpt-4o-mini added extra variables. Giving the correct matrix to the broad approach did not change MSO results much. In conflict tests a rising score with complexity is an artifact of poor scores when the true conflict count is zero.
numbers: Metric rule: if both ground truth and output are empty, precision and recall are set to 1.
limits: Empty-conflict cases blur averages.
agent_relevance: Test the agent on cases with no conflict too; scoring empty-equals-empty as perfect hides over-reporting.

source: Plank & Wotawa (2026), framing of the 2025 study
finding: Plank and Wotawa say the 2025 study mainly looked at LLMs as support inside model-based diagnosis, and ask directly whether LLMs diagnose on their own. A ChatGPT chat (April 2026) gave only correct diagnoses on a classic circuit; they guess hidden diagnostic procedures may be involved.
numbers: Single ChatGPT conversation; no count.
limits: Anecdote and speculation; the authors call for a larger study with parametrised circuit sizes.
agent_relevance: Gap: no published test of an LLM agent running the full conflict, hitting-set, test-selection loop at scale.

source: Search note for Angle A: LLM plus hitting-set tree papers
finding: Six web searches and three API tries (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, arXiv all returned rate-limit errors). No paper found that tests an LLM agent building Reiter HS-trees. Only the two DX papers (a17, a18, a20) touch LLMs and Reiter diagnosis. LLM fault localisation work for software appeared in results but was not opened and does not use hitting sets.
numbers: n/a
limits: A gap in my search is not proof that none exists.
agent_relevance: Using a hitting-set tree to control an LLM search over suspects looks new.

source: Abreu & van Gemund (2009) Staccato approximate hitting set, as described by Pill et al. 2016
finding: Staccato ranks components by how many unhit conflicts they appear in, takes the top ones, and runs a heuristic-limited search on a binary matrix. It is approximate and results must be verified for minimality.
numbers: In Pill et al. 2016 their Staccato implementation could not even solve the smallest TSA2 samples and was excluded.
limits: That failure is for their Python version; the original paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: Ranking suspects by how many contradictions they appear in is a cheap ordering rule, but needs a minimality check afterward.

source: Lin & Jiang (2003) Boolean-algebra hitting sets (BHS-tree), as described by Pill et al. 2016
finding: Boolean algorithm: split on an element; conflicts containing it are hit, the rest form a second branch. Needs all conflicts known in advance, unlike HS-DAG or HST.
numbers: See a08 for the benchmark. Pill and Quaritsch (2012) found choosing the split element from a smallest conflict improves it a lot.
limits: Only a second-hand description.
agent_relevance: Choose the branch element from the smallest unresolved contradiction: a cheap rule for the agent.

source: de Kleer & Williams (1987) Diagnosing multiple faults (GDE), as reported in Rodler 2019 and Pill et al. 2016
finding: GDE was the parallel foundation. It tracks candidates and conflicts with bookkeeping rather than a black-box reasoner, and uses entropy to pick the next measurement. GDE-style tools prevail in circuits; HS-Tree tools in knowledge-based systems.
numbers: In Pill et al. 2016, GDE beat all rivals up to about 30 components (10 ms) and tracked HS-DAG closely for large conflict sets with lower memory.
limits: GDE paper not opened; glass-box, so less general than HS-Tree.
agent_relevance: Entropy-based test choice is the natural step after the suspect tree: pick the test that splits the suspect mass most evenly.

source: Rodler (2020) measurement selection heuristics ENT, SPL, MPS used with HS-Tree
finding: ENT is the entropy rule of de Kleer and Williams; SPL is split-in-half (prefers the test eliminating the most diagnoses in the worst case); MPS is most probable singleton. DynamicHS runtime gains did not differ by heuristic.
numbers: Medians: ENT 50%, SPL 52%, MPS 52% runtime saving.
limits: Quality of the chosen test sequence is studied elsewhere, not in this paper.
agent_relevance: Cheap default for the agent: split-in-half over the current suspect list.

source: Plank & Wotawa (2026) evaluation design
finding: Scoring: six categories on a 0-2 scale; weights correctness 30%, reasoning 20%, hallucination 20%, completeness 15%, uncertainty 10%, clarity 5%. Correctness is judged against the set of subset-minimal diagnoses for each scenario.
numbers: 10 small and 3 large models; rank-sum across circuits also computed; top three models below 0.47 mean standard deviation, most small models above 0.6.
limits: Manual evaluation, possible bias, acknowledged by the authors.
agent_relevance: Using the minimal diagnosis set as the gold answer gives a clear grading target for our benchmark.
